Science.title: Even parasites have parasites: Fungus infects powdery mildew
Science.summary: In the fungal kingdom, no one is safe from parasites—not even other parasites. A new study from North Carolina State University finds that Ampelomyces, an intracellular fungus that infects the plant disease powdery mildew, is far more common than previously known. By screening museum samples of powdery mildews up to about 150 years old, researchers discovered that not only is Ampelomyces quite common, but many specimens labeled as Ampelomyces are misidentified.

Science.title: Validation of clinical and preclinical obesity across global cohorts
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11237-5 A large-scale data analysis assesses the Lancet Commission’s proposed diagnostic framework for obesity, finding that this framework, in which BMI is combined with other criteria, such as waist circumference and organ function, is more useful than classifications based on BMI alone.

Science.title: Chip identifies cells by their electrical signature, then separates them with a precisely aimed sound wave
Science.summary: In biomedicine, sorting cells accurately without damaging them remains a persistent problem. Current methods, like fluorescence-activated cell sorting, rely on labeling the cells extrinsically, which can stress the cells, alter their behavior and even interfere with the assay. A collaborative study between researchers in Singapore and China has now developed a noninvasive, label-free method to sort cells.

Science.title: NASA reveals Earth's ozone hole has grown to a size not seen in a decade
Science.summary: The Antarctic ozone hole expanded to its seventh-largest size on record in 2026, driven by unusual weather conditions that pushed it close to its historic maximum. Scientists say international restrictions on ozone-destroying chemicals prevented even greater damage, and Earth's protective ozone layer is still recovering.

Science.title: Did comets bring building blocks of life to Earth? Scientists aren't so sure anymore
Science.summary: For over a century astronomers have speculated that comets could have delivered organic molecules necessary for life to Earth, but new modeling shows these molecules wouldn't have survived impact.

Science.title: New culprit in early Alzheimer’s: Blood–brain barrier blocks protective proteins
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03655-2 The brain relies on crucial proteins to maintain neurons. This system is disrupted in mice with neurological disease.

Science.title: Deep-sea mollusk houses bacteria in tiny 'dragon balls,' revealing a new symbiotic structure
Science.summary: Researchers at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) have discovered a previously unknown specialized organelle structure in a deep-sea mollusk living at cold seeps in the South China Sea. Dedicated to maintaining bacterial symbiosis, this newly identified survival mechanism provides new insights into how deep-sea organisms adapt to nearly oxygen-free environments and opens new directions for research on chemosymbiosis, organelle evolution and deep-sea ecosystems.

Science.title: Scientists discover why some mosquitoes love you and others don't
Science.summary: A surprising new study reveals that mosquitoes have very different tastes in humans, with each species attracted to its own combination of skin odors, chemicals, and bacteria. The discovery challenges the idea of a universal mosquito magnet and could lead to more effective repellents against dangerous disease-spreading mosquitoes.

Science.title: Clean water, hidden risks: New technology reveals neurotoxicity missed by conventional water quality monitoring
Science.summary: A photograph of an orchestra can tell you whether the musicians are on stage and their instruments are intact. But it cannot tell you whether they are playing in harmony. Even when every musician is present, a subtle loss of coordination can change the entire performance.

Science.title: Where are all the males? Ancient human fossils reveal a startling mystery
Science.summary: A remarkable discovery in a South African cave suggests that an extinct human relative may have created an all-female burial site more than 240,000 years ago. Scientists analyzed ancient proteins preserved in Homo naledi teeth and found no male-specific markers among at least 20 individuals, potentially solving a mystery that has puzzled researchers for over a decade.

Science.title: Non-halogen aqueous electrolytes for four-electron iodine conversion
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11282-0 An electrolyte framework that harnesses anionic chemistry to coordinate the interfacial microenvironment and molecular interactions enables reversible four-electron iodine conversion in halogen-free aqueous electrolytes, and is validated in metal–iodine batteries.

Science.title: Epigenetic heterogeneity in breast tumours informs diagnosis and prognosis
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11230-y Single-cell epigenetic analyses reveal a conserved epigenetic signature across patients that may help identify those at increased risk for disease relapse in breast cancer.

Science.title: New method maps DNA folding and epigenetic marks in single cells
Science.summary: A new experimental procedure developed by researchers at Yale School of Medicine could help scientists better understand how DNA structure influences disease and development.

Science.title: Scientists discover a giant 66-pound rodent that lived 34 million years ago
Science.summary: Scientists have uncovered fossils of a giant rodent that lived in Thailand 34 million years ago, revealing that enormous rodents evolved much earlier than previously thought. Named Yakamys sirindhornae, the ancient animal may have weighed around 66 pounds, roughly twice as much as other known rodents of its time.

Science.title: 237-million-year-old fossils reveal a bizarre armored sea amphibian
Science.summary: A bizarre, heavily armored amphibian roamed the oceans 237 million years ago, despite the fact that modern amphibians cannot survive entirely in saltwater. Discovered in China, the giant salamander-sized creature may be the first known amphibian to have adapted to a fully marine existence.

Science.title: Human replisomes direct a dedicated leading-strand primase for fork restart
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11204-0 Structural and biochemical studies show that the CMG helicase directly recruits PRIMPOL for leading-strand repriming, enabling replication fork restart and limiting post-replicative DNA gaps.

Science.title: Human land use drives microplastic abundance in terrestrial wildlife
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11285-x Microplastic burdens in Brazilian tapirs and anteaters rise with human-modified land use and proximity to development, however animals in remote habitats also carry microplastics, showing that landscape change and individual space use jointly shape wildlife exposure.

Science.title: Biodegradable bubble moves away from lactic acid without a motor—a step toward artificial cells
Science.summary: A tiny biodegradable bubble can move away from a chemical on its own, without a motor. Living cells need complex molecular machinery to do this. This discovery by researchers led by chemist Daniela Wilson at Radboud University, together with colleagues at Durham University, is a step toward artificial cells with lifelike behavior and could, in the long term, provide an interesting approach for self-steering particles in targeted drug delivery.

Science.title: 'No one dared question his results': How thermodynamics sparked a heated debate about Earth's age in the 19th century
Science.summary: In this excerpt from "This is Life: A Journey from Inside Your Body to Beyond Earth," author and physicist Christophe Galfard explores the way 19th century scientists were starting to use thermodynamics to understand just how old Earth is.

Science.title: When rain finally does come to drylands, only some microbes in the soil 'awaken'
Science.summary: In arid regions, the microbes that power threatened dryland soil ecosystems called biological soil crusts stay dormant over long periods, only "awakening" when they sense moisture from infrequent rainfall. Now, a team led by researchers at Penn State—driven by projections that those biocrusts will decline by as much as 40% in the next 45 years—found that when a dryland soil does get wet, most of the microbes in the biocrust stay inactive. It's a discovery that will inform ongoing efforts to conserve and restore biocrusts, according to the researchers.

Science.title: Spain's massive stone tombs reveal collective burials continued well into Bronze Age
Science.summary: Iberian people continued using, and possibly building, massive necropolises well into the Bronze Age, according to a study published in PLOS One by Eduardo Vijande-Vila of the University of Cádiz, Spain, and colleagues.

Science.title: The Grand Canyon is missing over a billion years of rocks. Now scientists know why.
Science.summary: The mission 1.2 billion years of geological history at the Grand Canyon finally has an explanation.

Science.title: Physicists propose new quantum device to measure how Earth twists space-time
Science.summary: A proposed tabletop quantum sensor could match the precision of the best satellite measurements of frame dragging, a subtle effect predicted by Einstein's general relativity.

Science.title: Monkey foot and palm prints differ between individuals, as they do in humans
Science.summary: In three species of monkey, the complex pattern of ridges on the feet and palms varies between individuals, similar to human fingerprints, according to a study published in the open-access journal PLOS One by Juliana Vieira Flores Sales at Universidade de Brasília and colleagues.

Science.title: Re-analysis of black hole data proves iconic ring shape really is there
Science.summary: The doughnut shape of the Event Horizon Telescope’s first image of a black hole has come under fire, but an independent check showed that it – and general relativity – still stands

Science.title: New study maps the genetic landscape of bovine TB across Wales
Science.summary: Bovine tuberculosis is evolving in different ways across different regions in Wales, according to the most detailed analysis of the bacterium conducted to date. One of the most significant animal health challenges facing Wales, bovine TB affects cattle health and farm businesses and places considerable emotional, social and financial pressures on farming communities.

Science.title: Salty grains in Saturn’s outermost ring formed from the slow freeze of plumes from the moon Enceladus
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03489-y One of Saturn’s rings consists of a diverse population of icy and rocky grains, each with a distinct composition. How this came about might now have an explanation.

Science.title: A distant exoplanet mysteriously vanished from sight. Astronomers just discovered why
Science.summary: Astronomers have solved the mystery of an exoplanet that "disappeared" after seven years of observations.

Science.title: Proposed approach for diagnosing obesity outperforms old method
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03425-0 A framework for diagnosing obesity that was proposed in 2025 incorporates waist circumference and related measures and distinguishes clinical from preclinical obesity on the basis of obesity-induced organ dysfunction. In an international multi-cohort study of 844,108 adults, this framework outperformed conventional body-mass-index-based criteria in diagnosing obesity and stratifying mortality risk.

Science.title: Domain-alteration chimeras rewire oncogenic complexes in prostate cancer
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11262-4 A novel therapeutic modality enforces non-native androgen receptor (AR)–p300/CBP interactions to collapse AR transcriptional programs, producing super-inhibitory, lineage-selective suppression of metastatic prostate cancer and establishing domain-alteration chimeras as a broadly applicable therapeutic strategy leveraging induced proximity.

Science.title: 2,200-year-old gold bear figurine and surprising number of bones found in massive burial mound in Kazakhstan
Science.summary: Archaeologists have found a 2,200-year-old golden bear in an Iron Age burial in Kazakhstan that may have held seven people.

Science.title: Florida's 'dark magic' mushrooms have a deadly combination of chemicals never seen before
Science.summary: Scientists have discovered that a known mushroom, Galerina indica , contains both psychedelic chemicals and deadly toxins.

Science.title: Microplastics change the colour of the sea near the Great Pacific Garbage Patch
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03637-4 The waters around the zone of floating debris appear greener and bluer on account of high levels of tiny bits of plastic.

Science.title: UNC13A splice correction rescues synaptic dysfunction induced by TDP-43 loss
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11256-2 TDP-43 loss induces a predegenerative state in which neurons remain structurally intact and suffer a substantial breakdown in synaptic communication; a therapeutic strategy is found that corrects UNC13A cryptic splicing by using splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides.

Science.title: NRF2 is a mechanosensitive checkpoint for NLRP3 inflammasome activation
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11324-7 The stiffness of the extracellular matrix is identified as a pivotal factor that influences activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in vitro and in vivo.

Science.title: Low-power 2D CFETs using single-crystal high- κ dielectrics
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11272-2 A transferable single-crystal anatase titanium dioxide dielectric enables high-quality interfaces with two-dimensional semiconductors, yielding near-ideal switching, low hysteresis and ultra-low-power complementary transistors and inverters.

Science.title: Evolutionary dynamics in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11269-x The somatic evolutionary histories of haematopoietic cells in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia diagnosis show that the clonal dynamics of blood comply with a set of simple evolutionary rules.

Science.title: Misunderstandings about statistics common even among experienced researchers
Science.summary: Even researchers and people with extensive training in statistics often find it difficult to interpret statistical results correctly. This is shown by a new systematic review carried out by Uppsala University and others, in which researchers have analyzed 55 studies involving over 15,000 participants. The work is published in PLOS One.

Science.title: Biologists reveal chlorophyll-building enzyme's structure for first time and clarify its mechanism
Science.summary: Plants are green because of a pigment that is key to photosynthesis: chlorophyll. In its production, the enzyme chlorophyll synthase plays an important role. As part of an international collaboration, researchers from Osnabrück University, the Center Algatech in Třeboň and the University of Sheffield have now succeeded in deciphering the structure of this enzyme and gaining valuable insights into its mechanism. The findings are published in the journal Nature Chemical Biology.

Science.title: Scientists uncover a 192-year-old mystery hidden in a mangled silver coin
Science.summary: A bizarrely deformed 1834 British silver coin found at a car boot sale may preserve evidence of a rare minting accident nearly 200 years ago. Advanced 3D scans and microscopic analysis revealed unusual metal distortions suggesting the coin was crushed under extreme pressure, potentially during its original production.

Science.title: The molecular basis of replication fork restart via repriming by PRIMPOL
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11276-y PRIMPOL is recruited to stalled forks through an interaction with the replicative helicase CDC45–MCM2–7–GINS, facilitating primer handover from PRIMPOL to the high-fidelity polymerase ε, minimizing mutagenic DNA synthesis.

Science.title: Mitochondrial protein import defects enhance tumour immunogenicity
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11249-1 Inhibition of mitochondrial protein import can enhance tumour immunogenicity by promoting mitochondrial DNA release.

Science.title: Looping DNA may help flowers grow nectar-producing organs
Science.summary: Nectaries are specialized floral tissues that secrete nectar to attract pollinators. Although the protein CRABS CLAW (CRC) is established as essential for nectary formation, the exact molecular mechanisms governing how it drives organ growth and secretion have remained unknown.

Science.title: Too dry for cacti: extreme droughts could push iconic species to extinction
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03671-2 Analysis reveals these plants face severe habitat loss across the Americas — plus, researchers test a new way to diagnose obesity.

Science.title: What is science? Even scientists can't agree
Science.summary: Scientists spend their careers trying to understand the world, but a new study suggests they have surprisingly different ideas about what science itself is. The study, published in Royal Society Open Science, found that scientists disagree about the meaning and purpose of science even more than the general public does. Of the 18 descriptions of science examined, few received unqualified endorsement from scientists, who often expressed reservations even about ideas they generally agreed with.

Science.title: NASA kick-starts a fresh push to bring Mars samples home
Science.summary: NASA is kickstarting a new initiative for Mars Sample Return (MSR), called the Perseverance Sample Retrieval Architecture.

Science.title: Extraordinary materials shaped by the principles of complex networks
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03272-z Network science has inspired the design of materials that spread out their deformation when a force is applied, have tunable stiffness and can control vibrational waves.

Science.title: Author or just ‘acknowledged’? How women are not gaining full credit for research
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03448-7 An analysis of who is more likely to get authorship than acknowledgement highlights the influence of a researcher’s gender and status.

Science.title: Scale-rich network-based metamaterials
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11191-2 A network-science-based framework that embeds network heterogeneity into mechanical metamaterials is used to produce scale-rich metamaterials that exhibit properties inaccessible to traditional single-scale systems.

Science.title: Metasurface waveguides for all-day augmented reality glasses
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11277-x An all-day-wearable augmented reality glasses prototype using a dual-layer metasurface-based waveguide and three matched grating patterns achieves a 30° field of view in an 8 × 8-mm2 two-dimensional eyebox while maintaining high luminance efficiency.

Science.title: Living with humility took on social weight in the late Middle Ages, historian argues
Science.summary: We're deep in the Middle Ages. In the mind's eye, monks stagger past, flagellating themselves to cleanse their sins and demonstrate their humility before God and creation. This was a time when humility—humilitas—was considered one of the fundamental virtues of Christian life.

Science.title: Superconducting vortices provide experimental evidence that clogging is a phase transition
Science.summary: Clogging is a phenomenon in which moving particles get stuck, slowing or blocking the flow, but how this transition occurs has remained experimentally unproven. Researchers from Science Tokyo studied superconducting vortices to demonstrate that clogging is a nonequilibrium phase transition. Using a two-step measurement protocol, they distinguished clogging from conventional pinning and revealed that both transitions share a critical point, offering new insights into predicting and controlling clogging across diverse systems.

Science.title: How pipes became status symbols in 18th-century Sweden
Science.summary: In the 18th century, a clay tobacco pipe could reveal more than you might think. Its length, quality and condition, as well as the way it was used, could signal social status. In a new doctoral thesis, Lund University archaeologist Robert Bergman Carter shows how smokeways at the time served as clear markers of status.

Science.title: Move over BMI: new obesity definition is better for predicting your health
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03636-5 A fresh approach considers waist circumference, rather than just weight and height, providing a more accurate classification.

Science.title: Rattlesnakes have personalities too — to venomous effect
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03536-8 A snake’s defensiveness might affect how much venom it produces in a laboratory test.

Science.title: Why holding on to loyal donors is not the right advice for every nonprofit
Science.summary: As humanitarian funding shrinks, conventional fundraising wisdom says to hold on to loyal donors. But new research shows that the value of a donor depends on how a nonprofit is set up. For many organizations, winning new donors matters more than keeping loyal ones.

Science.title: Scientists challenge the dream of bringing extinct species back to life
Science.summary: Could extinction itself become a thing of the past? Advances in biotechnology, including ancient DNA sequencing, genome analysis and gene editing, have led some to believe that it may be possible to bring extinct species back to life.

Science.title: A man swallowed a bone, and‬ 15 years later, doctors found it in his appendix
Science.summary: A man's appendix had to be removed, but not for dangerous inflammation, as you might expect.

Science.title: Efficient catalyst-controlled C–H arylation of arenes
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11391-w Efficient catalyst-controlled C–H arylation of arenes

Science.title: We can't see Fast Radio Bursts but we can now hear them thanks to a Finnish Cathedral
Science.summary: Fast radio bursts are invisible, but a composer has turned thousands of them into sound at a Finnish cathedral, where a choir will sing along on Nov. 21.

Science.title: Uranus has a weird magnetic field that's stumped scientists for 40 years — we may finally know why
Science.summary: The lopsided magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune could be the product of extreme conditions inside the planets, increasing the electrical conductivity that enhances the dynamo effect.

Science.title: Andy Weir's 'Exoplanet' just landed on Audible, but what actually makes an exoplanet habitable?
Science.summary: How would the crew of the Wild Blue Yonder fare on a real exoplanet?

Science.title: Retractions of old papers are on the rise: when should bad science be culled?
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03624-9 Decades-old papers are increasingly being pulled from the literature, bringing a host of challenges.

Science.title: Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose, and John Leguizamo reveal why they joined Andy Weir's sci-fi audio drama 'Exoplanet' (interview)
Science.summary: We hooked up with Mackie, DeBose, and Lequizamo to learn more about this renaissance of audio dramas and what attracted them to board Weir's sci-fi thriller.

Science.title: How I balance my life as a professional surfer and a university researcher
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03183-z Cliff Kapono shares his advice on ways to navigate and grow two different careers.

Science.title: How to avoid aliens and live
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03515-z Silence is golden.
